full_judgment:
2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that the appellants as plaintiffs filed SCC Suit No.4 of 1995 in the Court of Assistant Judge and SCC Judge, Faridpur Sadar against the respondents as defendants for a decree for ejectment. Subsequently, the case was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge No.1, Faridpur and renumbered as SCC Suit No.6 of 1996. The suit premises constitute a portion of Municipal Holding No. 133/1, known as Room No.5 of the said holding belonged to Abdul Aziz and another from whom the plaintiffs purchased the same by three registered kabalas dated 31-8-1994, 28-9-1994 and 02-11-1994 and got delivery of possession. Prior to their purchase, the defendants were tenants in respect of the suit premises, a shop room, at a monthly rent of Taka 200 payable according to Gregorian Calendar under an agreement dated 26-2-1987; that following the purchase of the plaintiffs Janab Hafez Tamizuddin, constituted attorney of the plaintiffs' vendors introduced the plaintiff No.1 with all the existing tenants including the respondents with instruction to pay the rent to the plaintiff No. 1 and to execute fresh lease agreement with the said purchasers, which the defendants agreed to do but as they did not act according to their promise and did neither pay any rent nor enter into any agreement and thus became defaulter; that the plaintiffs after duly terminating the tenancy by service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 filed the suit for a decree for ejectment. 

 3. The respondents as defendants contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable; that the defendants obtained lease of the suit premises from Hafez Md Tamizuddin, attorney for the owners Abdul Aziz and another i.e. the plaintiffs' predecessor initially at a monthly rent of Taka 150, which was later enhanced to Taka 200 per month under an agreement for lease dated 26- 2-1987 together with consideration of Taka 17,000 for possession on condition to pay the rent for each month within three days of the month next following; that the defendants regularly paid the rent without any receipt upto 03-10-1994 and on that date the defendants obtained an acknowledgement in writing from the said attorney Tamizuddin; that in view of non-acceptance of the rent on 3-1-1995 the defendants remitted the rent by money order on 10-1-1995 and in view of refusal by the landlord to receive the same they deposited the same with the Rent Controller and Senior Assistant Judge, Faridpur Sadar in Miscellaneous Case No.3 of 1995; that on receipt of the notice of the said suit, the landlord contested the same by filing written objection wherein the factum of sale of the suit holding was disclosed for the first time; that thereafter the defendants sent the rent on 9-4-1995 by money order to the plaintiffs of the SCC Suit and on refusal added the plaintiffs as opposite parties in the House Rent Case and, as such, the defendants are not defaulters; that the plaintiffs did not serve any notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act,1882 and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 (1) whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in failing to notice that the agreement of lease (Exhibit A) is a void agreement, being hit by section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 read with section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872 in consequence of which the status of the tenants becomes that of a monthly tenant as per the pro-position laid down by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in a number of cases including the cases reported in 31 DLR (AD) 155. 

 (II) whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in holding without any justification that the tenants in the instant case are non-evictable tenants and are not liable to be evicted by giving notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 which is absolutely unwarranted and against the law and will have the effect of making the landlord a rent receiver and equating the lease of a premises with permanent lease with no remedy available to the landlord against defaulting tenants. 

 7. Mr Nur Hossain Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants submits that the High Court Division erred in law in failing to notice that the agreement for lease (Exhibit- A) is a void agreement, being hit by section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 read with section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872 in consequence of which the status of the tenants becomes that of a monthly tenant. In support of his contention he has cited the decision reported in 31 DLR (AD) 155. He then submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the tenants in the instant case are non-evictable tenants and are not liable to be evicted by giving notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 which is absolutely unwarranted and against the law and will have the effect of making the landlord a rent receiver. He further submits that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law basing his decision on the agreement for lease (Exhibit A) against the mandate of the statute and in making out a third case of usage, there being no such case either in the pleading or in the evidence, in derogation of the statutory law. He finally submits that the case raises questions of law of public importance as to the interpretation of the law relating to lease of premises, in particular section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991, section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872 and the related provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and, as such, the appeal is liable to be allowed. 

 8. In the instant case it appears that admittedly the appellants are the owners of the premises by three purchase deeds dated 31-8-1994, 28-9- 1994 and 02-11-1994 and got delivery of possession and admittedly prior to their purchase, the respondents were tenants in the suit premises, a shop room at a monthly rent of Taka 200. It is the case of the appellants that the respondents were introduced to the appellants by the vendor who asked them to pay rent to the appellants to which they agreed; that the respondents became defaulter in making payment of rent which caused the appellant to terminate the tenancy by serving notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and filed the SCC Suit. The contention of the respondents as appears from their written statement and evidence is that they are not defaulter rather they purchased possession of the suit premises from the vendor of the appellant with a cash of Taka 17,000 and agreed to pay rent of Taka 200 per month. The agreement (Exhibit-A) in respect of sale of possession of the premises by the vendor of the appellants to the respondents is a void agreement being hit by section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 which provides that the landlord shall not claim, receive or invite offers or asked for any premium, jamanat, salami, fine or any other like sum in addition to the rent in consideration of the grant, renewal or continuance of a tenancy of any premises. Section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872 precisely provides that the consideration or object of an agreement is lawful unless it is forbidden by law. Therefore no suit lies to enforce an illegal contract. According to section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 the respondents alleged agreement (Annexure-A) is a void agreement because of the provision of section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 read with section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872 in consequence of which the status of the tenants becomes a monthly tenant. In this regard it is pertinent to refer to the decision of the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed vs Mohd Hassan reported in 31 DLR (AD) 155 where tenancy was created for a period of two years. In clause 1 of the agreement it was not mentioned that the appellant was taking the premises at a monthly rent of Taka 1,600 payable according to Gregorian Calendar month. Clause 2 of the agreement mentions the payment of an advance of Taka 19,200 out of which an amount of Taka 800 will be deducted every month towards the payment of rent. After the advance has been deducted in this way within a period of twenty four months the tenant will pay rent at Taka 1600 in cash every month. This Division held that Clause (a) of section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance,1963 prohibits the acceptance of any sum of money over and above the rent payable by a tenant. This clause has also made illegal even any claim or invitation of an offer for the payment of such sum of money in the form of premium, salami or fine either when tenancy is being created or renewed, or during its continuance. Under Clause (b) no one is allowed to claim or receive a payment of more than one month's rent in advance. The Appellate Division further held that the agreement for lease was void under section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872 as its object was not lawful and that it having not been registered was unenforceable and also inadmissible in evidence. The agreement to pay Taka 19,200 by way of advance rent was undoubtedly a part of the consideration of the transaction as defined in section 2(d) of the Contract Act, 1872. This contravenes the positive statutory mandate as provided in section 10(b) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963. In view of the unenforceability of the agreement the position is that the appellants are monthly tenant who is liable to ejectment if he makes default in payment of rent as provided in section 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. This Division further held that as long as the respondents had the unadjusted amount in their hands, they could have adjusted it towards the payment of rent for the months of October, November and December. In view of the provisions of section 18(5) of the Ordinance which do not seem to have been contravened by the appellant no default appears to have been made by him in paying the rent for the months of October, November and December, 1973. 

 9. In the instant case it appears that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in failing to notice that the agreement of lease (Exhibit-A) is a void agreement in view of section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 read with section 23 of the Contract Act,1872. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division also failed to notice that the respondents are monthly evictable tenants and, as such, they are liable to be evicted by giving notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 which is attracted in the facts and circumstances of the case. On perusal of the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the learned Judge of SCC Court has found that admittedly the appellants are the owners of the premises by purchase and the respondents are tenants under the appellants. It has also been found by the Court below that the respondents by failing to make payment of rent within the stipulated period became defaulter as a result of which a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 was duly served upon them and consequently the SCC Suit was filed against them.
